{"status":"ok","message-type":"work-list","message-version":"1.0.0","message":{"facets":{},"next-cursor":"MjUuODgwNTI3LDE3NzA4MzQxNzYwMDAsMTAuMTM3MSUyRmpvdXJuYWwucG9uZS4wMzQyNjIy","total-results":30507,"items":[{"group-title":"SSRN","publisher":"Elsevier BV","license":[{"start":{"date-parts":[[2026,1,1]],"date-time":"2026-01-01T00:00:00Z","timestamp":1767225600000},"content-version":"unspecified","delay-in-days":0,"URL":"https://www.uspto.gov/ip-policy/copyright-policy/copyright-basics"}],"abstract":"The article addresses the gap between the distributed production of action and the addressed nature of its consequences. In a sociotechnical network a text, a decision, and a publication are produced distributively, while harm occurs in addressed form; ordinary and legal thinking fill this gap with the question "who is the author?" — and discover that there is no answer. We distinguish three positions that may coincide but need not: the presenter, the bearer of the duty to answer, and the bearer of the restorative obligation. The thesis defended is that the restorative obligation is not automatically exhausted by authorship, causal contribution, or control over a particular action, and therefore cannot be secured by merely strengthening ex ante control. §2 situates the move within the debate on the responsibility gap, distinguishing the ascription of an action, the answer to a challenge, and restoration. §3 shows that presentation is neither a sufficient nor a necessary condition of the restorative obligation. §4 derives the conditions of enforceability of restoration (bearer, trace, criterion of completion) and introduces the normative principle of predictable addressed risk. §5 gives a criterion for distributing obligations among the positions of the network. §6 applies the scheme to correction and retraction, introducing the retraction norm from speech-act theory together with a criterion of proportionality. §7 examines the hard case of the retraction of a scientific publication. §8 fixes the main consequence: responsibility is not reducible to authorship. The result is not a demonstration of three necessary conditions as a logical inevitability, but a normative criterion of design for restorative procedures.","DOI":"10.2139/ssrn.7516558","type":"posted-content","is-referenced-by-count":0,"title":["Restorative Obligation in Distributed Action: Presentation, Correction, and Retraction"],"author":[{"ORCID":"https://orcid.org/0009-0003-6286-1404","authenticated-orcid":true,"given":"Denis","family":"Vlasov","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"references-count":0,"URL":"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7516558"},{"group-title":"In Review","publisher":"Springer Science and Business Media LLC","license":[{"start":{"date-parts":[[2026,6,9]],"date-time":"2026-06-09T00:00:00Z","timestamp":1780963200000},"content-version":"unspecified","delay-in-days":0,"URL":"https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/"}],"abstract":"Abstract

Scientific misconduct exploits the very mechanisms through which science establishes credibility, yet scientific correction is still commonly reduced to retraction counts. Retractions, however, represent only one observable manifestation of a far more complex regulatory system. Here, we develop a multidimensional systems-level framework for understanding scientific correction across the global scientific enterprise immediately before the emergence of AI-driven scientific governance. Integrating publication and retraction data from the 58 largest national scientific systems during 1900–2025, we examine three interconnected dimensions of correction architecture: the dynamics of scientific correction itself, its macro-structural organization, and its political-economic configuration. To support this framework, we introduce new multidimensional indicators, including the Normalized Retraction Rate and Duration Index (NRRDI) and the Normalized Retraction Rate and Slope13 Index (NRS13I). Our analyses suggest that scientific correction is intrinsically multidimensional, comprising distinct but interconnected dimensions of retraction burden, correction latency, collaboration-dependent correction structure, and early correction concentration dynamics. Across national systems, higher observable correction frequency was consistently associated with shorter correction latency, suggesting that correction visibility and correction responsiveness represent complementary manifestations of regulatory capacity rather than simple indicators of scientific dysfunction. The findings further reveal a pronounced East–West bipolarity in the global geography of scientific correction: retraction burden was concentrated disproportionately within Eastern and Middle Eastern scientific systems, whereas prolonged correction latency was concentrated predominantly within Western systems. This dissociation motivated the Retraction Cascade Hypothesis (RCH), which proposes that historically elevated correction visibility may amplify future correction concentration through self-reinforcing surveillance and anomaly-detection processes. Strikingly, academic freedom exhibited one of the strongest and most consistent inverse associations with retraction burden and displayed a closely parallel geographic pattern, suggesting that global correction asymmetries arise not only from surveillance amplification but also from deeper differences in epistemic-governance environments. More broadly, scientific correction emerged as a structurally embedded property of national scientific systems linked to governance quality, human development, institutional coherence, and epistemic openness. Governance-related and human-capital dimensions consistently exhibited stronger associations with correction-system organization than economic scale alone, although substantial residual heterogeneity indicated that important components of correction dynamics remain only partially predictable from macro-structural conditions. Across all three analytical dimensions, countries organized into distinct latent global correction regimes characterized by different combinations of developmental conditions, governance architecture, collaboration structure, and corrective visibility. Political-economic analyses demonstrated that scientific correction exposure scales super-proportionally with economic and research-investment scale, while increased R&D intensity did not significantly attenuate this relationship. At the same time, several comparatively low-cost scientific systems exhibited high efficiency-adjusted publication productivity despite elevated correction exposure, indicating that economic efficiency and integrity stability are not synonymous organizational properties. Importantly, although the political economy of scientific correction provides valuable insight into correction-system organization, reducing scientific correction primarily to economic loss would constitute a substantial conceptual oversimplification. The measurable financial exposure associated with retractions remains proportionally negligible relative to broader research investment and likely represents only the visible component of a much larger epistemic problem whose hidden scientific, societal, and potentially economic consequences remain difficult to quantify. Together, these findings support a reconceptualization of scientific correction as an adaptive layer of epistemic governance rather than a simple accumulation of isolated retractions. Correction mechanisms appear not merely as retrospective instruments of error removal, but as structurally organized processes through which scientific systems regulate credibility, transparency, accountability, and epistemic self-correction under varying institutional and developmental conditions. By establishing a multidimensional empirical baseline for the pre-AI era, this study provides a foundation for evaluating how artificial intelligence may reshape the architecture of scientific self-regulation in the decades ahead.

Integr Peer Rev"],"abstract":"Abstract Background Conflicts of interest (CoI) can undermine trust in scientific publishing, yet empirical evidence on how often CoI lead to editorial action and how journals respond remains limited. This study aimed to characterise the frequency, patterns, and editorial handling of CoI‑related notices in the scholarly literature using an openly available, multidisciplinary dataset. Methods We conducted a descriptive cross‑sectional analysis of publicly available records from the Retraction Watch (RW) database, accessed via Crossref, from inception to 23 April 2026. All editorial notices in which CoI was explicitly mentioned as the sole or one of several stated reasons were included, encompassing retractions, corrections, expressions of concern, and reinstatements. For each record, we extracted article and notice dates, article type, scientific field, country of the corresponding author, number of authors and institutions, publisher, and all stated reasons for the notice. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and bootstrap‑based confidence intervals. Results We identified 886 CoI‑related records (748 retractions, 39 corrections, 97 expressions of concern, and 2 reinstatements). CoI was the sole stated reason in 95 cases (10.7%), including 32 retractions, 11 corrections, and 52 expressions of concern; in the remaining notices, CoI most commonly co‑occurred with concerns such as compromised peer review, authorship or affiliation problems, journal or institutional investigations, and broader ethical violations. The median time from publication to editorial action was longest for expressions of concern and shortest for corrections, with wide variability across records and notice types. CoI‑related notices were concentrated in basic life, biomedical, and health sciences, and were unevenly distributed across high‑output countries and a small number of large publishers, particularly open‑access outlets. Most affected articles were original research papers with multi‑author, multi‑institution teams. Among articles with determinable author gender, both first and last authors were more often male than female, although these patterns were exploratory and lacked a baseline comparator. Conclusions Editorial actions explicitly linked to CoI remain relatively uncommon compared with the broader volume of retractions and corrections, and CoI are rarely cited in isolation. The frequent co‑occurrence of CoI with other forms of misconduct or procedural problems suggests that undisclosed or poorly managed CoI often signal deeper weaknesses in disclosure practices, editorial oversight, and research governance rather than isolated administrative lapses. Strengthening CoI policies, transparency, verification mechanisms, and linked metadata systems may help detect problems earlier and support more consistent, graduated editorial responses. The effectiveness and safety of acellular dermal allografts for this condition remain uncertain. Objective This systematic review and single-arm meta-analysis aims to evaluate the effectiveness of acellular dermal allografts in correcting lower eyelid retraction. Methods A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane was performed to identify studies using acellular dermal allografts for lower eyelid retraction correction. Outcomes included margin reflex distance 2 (MRD2) improvement, inferior scleral show (ISS) improvement, complications, and reoperation rates. Statistical analyses were conducted using R Studio, and heterogeneity was assessed with I 2 statistics. Results Fifteen studies with 330 participants (413 eyelids) were included. The pooled mean change in MRD2 was 2.12 mm (95% CI, 1.63–2.61 mm; I 2 = 94.69%, P < 0.001), reduced to I 2 = 66% after excluding Graves' disease–only studies. ISS improved by 2.21 mm (95% CI, 1.23–3.19 mm; I 2 = 96.22%, P < 0.001). Complication and reoperation rates were 8.97% and 0.04%, respectively. Common complications included granulomas, pain, tearing, and discharge. Conclusion Acellular dermal matrix grafts demonstrate the effectiveness and safety of lower eyelid retraction correction.
